ch.749: Name a child Hongyi, or just Hong or Yi. Hong is a wide heart, yi a tough spirit; together they are this line's meaning. Good for boys or girls.
ch.750: One line, four names: Zhidao, Jude, Yiren, Youyi. Siblings can take one each, and in order they make the sentence. Yi here means the six arts (ritual, music, archery, charioteering, writing, numbers), so Youyi is not about idle play.
ch.751: Names: Delin, Youlin, Bugu. Someone of virtue will always find people drawing near. Also a good name for a small shop or a community reading room.
ch.752: Names: Duzhi, Jinsi, Qiewen, Boxue. Jinsi means thinking from what is close at hand, not shallow thinking.
ch.753: Use song (pine) or bai (cypress) in a name; a study or shop can be called Houdiao or Suihan. The point: only in the cold do you see who does not wither, who can stand hardship.
ch.754: Names: Leshan, Leshui, Renjing. Le here means to delight in (read lè). The mountain stands for steadiness, water for flow; two children could take one each.
ch.755: Names: Minxing, Shenyan, Minzhi. Quick to act, careful in speech: for families who hope their child will be steady.
ch.756: Do not use qiaoyan (clever words) in a name: the line says such people are rarely humane.
ch.757: Do not use kengkeng in a name: it describes a narrow, rigid mind.
ch.758: Do not use xiangyuan in a name: Confucius calls the village worthy a thief of virtue.
ch.759: The first line of the Analects, the most natural choice for the start of school. For a child, add: learn it, then go and practise; once you can do it, you will be glad.
ch.760: Xi means practising again and again, not just reviewing the textbook.
ch.761: The best line for a teacher's first lesson: if you do not understand, raise your hand. Saying so is no shame; pretending to understand is what costs you.
ch.762: For a child starting a new class or choosing a major: knowing it is not as good as liking it; liking it is not as good as finding joy in learning it.
ch.763: For new classmates and roommates: everyone around you has something to learn from; when you see someone's fault, check whether you have it too.
ch.764: The second half says to correct what is not good in yourself; it is not only about finding good teachers.
ch.765: For older students preparing for exams: study as if you cannot catch up, and once you have, fear losing it.
ch.766: Can be made into a term plan: learn one new thing each day, and each month look back to see you have not forgotten. Wang here means wu, 'without'.
ch.767: For teachers and parents: help a child only when they are eager to work it out, or trying to say it and cannot. At the start of term, do not hand over every answer.
ch.768: Confucius starts from age fifteen. At a coming-of-age ceremony you can say: set your aim at fifteen, stand on your own at thirty, and the years between are yours.
ch.769: Li at thirty means standing firm with a mind of one's own, not only starting a family and a career.
ch.770: Being an adult means governing yourself. Yikonglu reads keji as restraining oneself: you manage your own conduct without waiting for others to. The following words, 'humaneness comes from oneself', say the same.
ch.771: For a child becoming independent: when things go wrong, first ask what you failed to do, then look at others.
ch.772: Pifu means an ordinary person, man or woman. The commander of a great army can be captured, but no one can take away an ordinary person's resolve.
ch.773: For a first job search or choosing a major: do not worry about having no position; worry about what qualifies you to stand in it.
ch.774: As an adult no one covers your mistakes. This line is five characters: when you err, do not fear to correct it.
ch.775: A graduation speech can give the original meaning: when your work is done well and you have strength left, keep learning; when your learning is solid and you have strength left, go and serve. Learning and doing alternate all your life.
ch.776: You means having strength to spare, not 'excellent grades'. Reading it as 'study well and you should become an official' gets it backwards.
ch.777: Best for a teacher seeing graduates off: how do we know your future will not surpass our present?
ch.778: The second half says that someone who has made no name by forty or fifty is not to be held in awe: it urges the young to work while they can, not only praises them.
ch.779: For those just entering working life: do not worry that no one knows you; go and know others, understand others.
ch.780: For students heading to work or graduate school. The rest of the line: serve the worthiest of the officials, befriend the most humane of the scholars. The best tools are good mentors and good friends.
ch.781: Originally Zigong asked how to practise humaneness, and Confucius used the craftsman as a comparison; it is not only about tools.
ch.782: Ideal for a class yearbook or graduation photo: friends gathered through study, and through friends we become better.
ch.783: A closing line for a graduation speech. Before it: a scholar must be broad and resolute, for the road is long and the load heavy.
ch.784: Zizhang asked how to seek office, and the answer is how to do a job: listen widely and set aside what you are unsure of, speak carefully even of what you are sure of; look widely and hold back from what you doubt. Few errors in speech, few regrets in action: there lies your living.
ch.785: Do the work in hand well first, then talk about pay. It does not say never discuss money; pay follows what you have done. Once the work is done, you can name your price with confidence.
ch.786: Three questions before leaving work: was I wholehearted in what I did for others? Did I keep my word to colleagues? Have I practised what I learned?
ch.787: For someone taking over a new project: rushing for results means none come; eyeing small gains means big things are not achieved.
ch.788: A workplace code in nine characters: be respectful at rest, earnest at work, wholehearted with people. Confucius says never drop these wherever you go.
ch.789: A newcomer should not decide things above their role; look after your own part.
ch.790: Often used to shirk: 'not my business'. The line already appears at 8.14, where Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: if those in office ask you, you must still tell them truthfully.
ch.791: Usable, but know its weight: Confucius ranks 'a sense of shame in conduct' and 'not disgracing the ruler's commission' first, and 'words must be trusted, deeds must be carried through' only third, calling such people kengkeng, which Zhu Xi reads as narrow.
ch.792: Keeping your word is the floor, not the highest praise; whether to do something depends on whether it is right, not on having said it.
ch.793: Yikonglu follows a Qing reading: this line is about husband and wife, valuing the other's virtue above looks. What follows covers serving parents, serving a ruler and friendship: four lines, four human bonds. A wedding officiant can start from here.
ch.794: Confucius chose a son-in-law by character alone. Gongye Chang was in prison at the time; Confucius said it was not his crime and gave him his daughter anyway. Told at a wedding by the bride's parents, it means: we chose you for who you are.
ch.795: Nan Rong kept reciting the ode about words that cannot be taken back, so Confucius gave him his niece in marriage. For the couple: in daily life, be careful in speech.
ch.796: For newlyweds: two people need not agree on everything; they can differ and still be in harmony. Going along with everything while resenting it inside is what disharmony really is.
ch.797: Harmony in the home is most precious. But the second half says harmony without measure will not work either. At a wedding, 'harmony is most precious' can be followed by 'talk things through, and keep to rules'.
ch.798: Often taken as 'smooth everything over'; the text in fact warns against seeking harmony at any cost.
ch.799: Guanju is the first ode of the Book of Songs, about a gentleman seeking a good wife. Confucius says it is joyful without excess, sorrowful without harm. If Guanju is read at a wedding, this line can follow.
ch.800: Confucius' wish: to give the old ease, friends trust, and the young care. At a one-month celebration, elders can say: now the family has one more little one to care for.
ch.801: A blessing for a newborn: who knows that this child will not surpass us as we are today?
ch.802: Confucius taught his son Kong Li only two things: study the Odes, or you will not know how to speak; study ritual, or you will not know how to stand. A family motto for a first birthday.
ch.803: Chen Kang suspected Confucius taught his son extra in private; he had not. He taught his son just as he taught his students, another point worth sharing with new parents.
ch.804: Can be written as a family motto: be filial at home, respectful outside, careful in action, true in speech, generous to all, close to the humane. It goes on: with strength to spare, study letters. Read books, but character comes first.
ch.805: Only at three does a child leave its parents' arms. New parents up at night with a baby will read this and know they were carried the same way.
ch.806: This comes from Confucius' dispute with Zai Wo over three years of mourning; its point is parents' kindness. On a card the line alone is fine, but leave out the mourning context.
ch.807: On New Year's Day, looking at the river. Zhu Xi reads it as heaven and earth never pausing, urging us never to pause in learning; most people today read it as time flowing away like water. Both fit the New Year: one is to cherish, the other is to keep going.
ch.808: For a year-end review: were you wholehearted for others? true to your friends? have you practised what you learned? Once a year is not enough; Zengzi asked himself daily.
ch.809: Write New Year plans under this line: a mound one basket short, and it is you who stopped; a single basket on level ground, and it is you who went forward. Success or not, it is up to you.
ch.810: For turning the page: last year's errors, once corrected, are gone; left uncorrected, they become true errors.
ch.811: The best line for going home for the New Year: remember your parents are a year older, glad of their long life and anxious that they are ageing.
ch.812: Write it on the new year's plan: without thought for what is far, trouble is close at hand.
ch.813: The safest line for a birthday of an elder: the humane live long. Before it: the wise delight in water, the humane in mountains, so a birthday couplet can start from mountains and water.
ch.814: By age: at fifty 'knowing the decree of heaven', at sixty 'an ear attuned', at seventy 'following the heart's desire without overstepping'. Confucius said these of himself; from the young to the old they are praise, not assessment.
ch.815: For elders still studying and busy: so absorbed he forgets to eat, so happy he forgets his worries, not noticing old age coming. Confucius said this was the kind of man he was.
ch.816: A rule for the birthday banquet: when villagers drank together, Confucius left only after the elders with staffs had gone. Young people should not leave the table first.
ch.817: Suited to the elder's own speech: in old age, remind yourself not to be grasping. It does not suit the young lecturing their elders with it.
ch.818: Never use this at a birthday.
ch.819: Here Confucius scolds one old acquaintance, Yuan Rang, who sat squatting waiting for him: not deferential as a youth, nothing to show as an adult, then he tapped his shin with his staff. The three lines go together and target this man, not all old people.
ch.820: When his student Boniu fell ill, Confucius visited and held his hand through the window. What matters most in visiting the sick is to go and to hold their hand.
ch.821: Confucius goes on to say 'we are losing him, it is fate', grief at knowing Boniu would die. Do not repeat this when visiting the sick.
ch.822: Illness is one of the three things Confucius was most careful about. For the patient's family: do not let illness drag on; follow the doctor's advice.
ch.823: When visiting a sick child or urging children to take care: parents can let go of everything except worry over their child's illness. Taking care of yourself is filial piety.
ch.824: Gravely ill, Confucius said he would rather die among his students than at the hands of retainers. The people at the bedside matter more than ceremony.
ch.825: When Confucius was ill and the ruler visited, he could not rise, so he laid his court robe over himself to receive him. The sick keep their dignity too, and visitors should leave them their dignity.
ch.826: Do not say this to someone who is ill.
ch.827: Zixia said this to console Sima Niu, who feared for his brothers; it is followed by 'the gentleman is reverent without fault, respectful and courteous to others'. Fate is not in our hands; what we can do is govern ourselves. Said alone to a patient, it sounds like telling them to give up.
ch.828: Most used in eulogies and funeral couplets: honour the departed with care, remember the distant ancestors, and people's hearts grow generous.
ch.829: Better true grief than a perfect funeral. A simple ceremony is fine so long as the heart is there.
ch.830: When Yan Yuan died, Confucius wept so hard his followers tried to calm him; he said: if not for this man, for whom should I grieve? For mourning a dearest friend.
ch.831: Confucius' first words on hearing of Yan Yuan's death: Heaven is destroying me. For losing a student or a companion on the way.
ch.832: Zhu Xi says Confucius grieved that the Way had no one to carry it on, not that he himself would die.
ch.833: Etiquette on the day of condolence: eating beside the bereaved, Confucius never ate his fill; on a day he had wept, he did not sing.
ch.834: When a friend died with no family to see to him, Confucius said: I will take care of the funeral. The weightiest words between friends.
ch.835: To comfort the bereaved: express your grief fully, but do not harm your health.
ch.836: Zhu Xi says the words 'and stop there' are a little brief, and may lead people to skip the details of ritual.
ch.837: The full statement on filial piety: in life, serve them by ritual; in death, bury them and sacrifice to them by ritual. For mourning parents.
ch.838: For a child going far away, always with the second half: if you go, let your parents know where. Today that means texting when you arrive and telling them when you move.
ch.839: Often only the first half is quoted, to stop someone leaving. Zhu Xi's point is not to leave your parents unable to find you, not that you may not go.
ch.840: Best for someone going abroad to work or study: treat people with respect and courtesy, and wherever you go there will be people like brothers.
ch.841: These are Zixia's words to console Sima Niu; first comes 'the gentleman is reverent without fault, respectful and courteous to others'. Only on that condition are all within the four seas brothers.
ch.842: For someone changing jobs or cities: what is past cannot be changed; what is to come can still be reached.
ch.843: This was sung to Confucius by the Chu recluse Jieyu, urging him to stop pursuing office; when Confucius wanted to speak to him, he hurried away. Fine to use in farewell, but do not present it as Confucius' words.
ch.844: When a friend takes a road you disagree with: advise sincerely, speak kindly; if they will not listen, stop, and do not let advice ruin the friendship.
ch.845: When parting, plan the next meeting: when you come back from afar, we will gather again.
ch.846: For when the fundamental paths differ and you cannot work together.
ch.847: Often used to part ways over small differences. Zhu Xi means the difference between good and evil, right and wrong; differences in method or opinion do not count.
